2 unchanged paragraphs, under In short {#short}

• **The passkey is what opens the vault.** With the WebAuthn PRF extension, a passkey returns 32 bytes that only your authenticator can produce, for this site, and the same bytes on every device the passkey syncs to.

• **Where is the top key stored? Nowhere.** sgit vault keys are made in the client, a passphrase and a vault id. So the browser computes the top vault's key and id from the PRF bytes, opens it, and finds every other key inside. No chicken and egg, no new storage, only vault APIs.

• **The top vault is a keyring, and the pattern is one we already use.** Vaults that hold the keys of other vaults, all the way down. The top holds the keys of your reading vault and your notes vault, the read keys you have been given, your access key, and your key pairs for this site.

• **The passkey is a lock, not an identity.** The key pairs are generated at random and stored in the top, never derived from the passkey. Change the lock and the identity is untouched.

• **Several passkeys, several tops.** An admin passkey on a hardware key and a reader passkey in the cloud open two different tops, chosen in the provider's own picker. Keys move between tops by copying; a top is retired by deleting its vault, after which its passkey opens nothing.

• **Recovery is the top key itself**, shown once and saved in a password manager. Lose the passkey and the saved key, and no one, including us, can open the vaults.

• **Support is good enough to build on, and where the passkey lives decides what the reader gets.** PRF works in Google Password Manager, iCloud Keychain, Windows Hello and Firefox. A synced provider or a hardware key gives the same newsroom on every device; a clean browser with neither gives one device, and Chrome's own store returns no PRF bytes at all, so the page checks at creation and offers a ladder of alternatives.

• **The passkey is what opens the vault, through a path.** With the WebAuthn PRF extension, a passkey returns 32 bytes that only your authenticator can produce for this site. The same passkey gives the same bytes on every device it syncs to, **through the same kind of path**. A different path, a phone answering a QR code instead of the provider on the device, can give different bytes, and in our test it did.

• **Where is the door key stored? Nowhere.** sgit vault keys are made in the client, a passphrase and a vault id. So the browser computes the door's key and address from the PRF bytes, opens it, and finds the master vault's key inside. No chicken and egg, no new storage, only vault APIs. The lab did this against a real vault server and opened the door again.

• **A door per set of bytes.** Every door holds the master's key and records its provider, its path, its credential id, the device and the date. The master lists its doors with their keys, so any door can be retired from any other.

• **Adding a door is a normal first-week step, and no key passes through a person.** While unlocked on a device where both paths run, a Mac with Chrome, ask for the bytes by the other path and the page writes the new door from memory. Where no device has both paths, the recovery code opens the recovery door and the new door is written from there.

• **"No door here yet" is not an error.** A device that derives an address and finds nothing is on a path that has no door. The page says so and offers the two ways in.

• **The master is the keyring, and the passkey is a lock, not an identity.** The master holds the keys of your reading vault and your notes vault, the read keys you have been given, your access key, and your key pairs, which are generated at random and never derived from the passkey. Change a lock and the identity is untouched.

• **Several passkeys for several roles are several masters.** An admin passkey on a hardware key and a reader passkey in the cloud open different masters, chosen in the provider's own picker. Keys move between masters by copying; a door is retired by deleting its one file, never by destroying its address.

• **Support is good enough to build on, and where the passkey lives decides what the reader gets.** PRF works in Google Password Manager, iCloud Keychain, Windows Hello and Firefox. The platform path is the common case: an iCloud Keychain passkey gave the same bytes on a Mac, an iPad and an iPhone, in Safari and in Chrome. A clean browser with no store gives one device, and Chrome's own store returns no PRF bytes, so the page checks at creation and offers a ladder.

3 unchanged paragraphs, under Part one: the design {#design}

### The test {#test}

The lab has seven cards: what the browser can do; make a passkey for this site with PRF; touch it and show a fingerprint of the bytes; derive the door; make a recovery code; compare the derivation with sgit's Python, value by value; and create the door on a vault server, open it again as a new device would, and delete its file. On 11 and 12 October it was run with one Google Password Manager passkey, made on the Mac and synced, and with one iCloud Keychain passkey.

What held:

• **The platform path.** The Google passkey gave the same bytes in Chrome on the Mac, answered by Google Password Manager with Touch ID, and in Safari on the iPhone, answered by the same provider with Face ID. The iCloud Keychain passkey gave the same bytes on the Mac, the iPad and the iPhone, in Safari and in Chrome.

• **The derivation.** From the bytes to a door address and passphrase, and from those to sgit's read and write keys, the browser and sgit's own Python agreed on every value, from a fixed test vector and from the live bytes.

• **The door.** With an access key, the page created the door at its derived address on the vault server, wrote its one file, the master's key encrypted under the door's read key, opened it again the way a new device would, and deleted the file.

What did not hold:

| Run | Client | How the passkey answered | Bytes | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | Chrome on a Mac | Google Password Manager on the Mac, Touch ID | A | | 2 | Safari on an iPhone | Google Password Manager on the phone, Face ID | A | | 3 | Safari on an iPad | A QR code, scanned by the iPhone; the phone's provider answered | B | | 4 | Chrome on the same Mac, "use a phone, tablet or security key" | A QR code, scanned by the same iPhone; the same provider answered | B |

Same credential id, same user handle, same input, same flags. Runs 1 and 2 share the platform path and share a result; runs 3 and 4 share the hybrid path and share the other. Run 1 and run 4 are the same browser on the same machine, minutes apart, differing only in which way the phone's provider was reached. Each path was deterministic; the two paths disagreed.

This is a known class of bug. Apple's developer forums carry the same symptom for iCloud Keychain passkeys since late 2024: one PRF value when the passkey is used on the device, another when an iPhone or iPad scans a QR code shown by a Mac, for the same credential and the same salt. An Apple engineer called it a bug, pointed at the extension's two seeds, one for when the user was verified and one for when not, and said a fix was in the iOS 18.4 and macOS 15.4 betas; a later tester reported it persisting. Our passkey was Google's, served to the QR flow through iOS's cross-device role for third-party providers, so either the bridge or the provider behaves differently on that path, and the lab cannot tell which. What it can tell, now, is which path a result came from, because the browser reports whether the authenticator was platform or cross-platform, and the card shows it.

The thing to notice is how long this has sat. A defect in the one property that makes PRF useful for encryption, visible to anyone who tries two paths, would not survive long under real load. The reasonable inference is that few people derive encryption keys from passkeys across the hybrid path in production. That is not a reason to avoid the technique. It is a reason to design as if the bytes are a key a provider lends for one path, and to keep every door replaceable.

1 unchanged paragraph

For the newsroom MVP, with the relying party ID `newsroom.sgit.ai`:

1. **The PRF input** is a fixed, public value: `SHA-256("newsroom.sgit.ai/top/v1")`. An input is not a secret; only the authenticator can turn it into the 32 bytes. 2. **The seed** is `HKDF-SHA256(ikm = PRF bytes, salt = SHA-256("newsroom.sgit.ai"), info = "sgit/top/v1")`. 3. **The passphrase and the vault id** are two more HKDF outputs from the seed. sgit accepts any printable ASCII passphrase up to 256 characters, so the passphrase is the hex of 32 bytes (`info = ".../passphrase"`), keeping all 256 bits. The vault id has to be lowercase letters and digits, 4 to 24 of them, so 8 characters are drawn from a third output (`info = ".../id"`) with rejection sampling, so that no character is favoured. 4. **The top vault key** is the sgit vault key made of those two, and from there, sgit's own derivation gives the read and write keys, exactly as the command line does: PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 at 600,000 iterations, once for the read key and once for the write key. That is the cost of this design. The top and the reading vault need up to four derivations; measured in headless Chromium on a four-core machine, one takes about 105 ms and six run together about 640 ms, and a phone is several times slower, so a cold unlock can spend a second or two deriving keys before it fetches anything. The brief measures it on a phone, derives each vault's keys once per session, runs them in a worker, and derives a write key only when there is something to write. 5. **A second compartment from the same passkey** is the same derivation with a different input, say `.../top/persona/v1`. Two inputs give two unrelated outputs and two tops. That separates what is in memory at once; it does not separate authority, because whoever can use the passkey gets both. Authority is separated by a second passkey, below. 6. **Collisions** are not a practical worry with 36⁸ possible ids, but the page checks: a derived id that already holds something it cannot open is skipped, with a counter in the HKDF info.

The browser and the command line must agree byte for byte, so the brief includes test vectors: the same inputs through the browser code and through sgit in Python, with the same keys out.

### What is in the top vault {#layout}

The top is a keyring: one small file of named entries, rarely written, and nothing else. The pattern is the one we already use everywhere, vaults that hold the keys of other vaults, so the only new thing here is where the top key comes from.

• **The keys of the vaults below it,** by site and purpose: the reading vault first, then the notes-to-the-agent vault, then whatever an agent creates for the reader. Each is an ordinary vault with its own random key, so a read key to one of them can be handed to an agent or a person without exposing anything above it. Depth is the blast radius control.

• **Read keys the reader has been given**, to vaults that belong to someone else.

• **The access key.** A read-only clone needs no token, so after the unlock the browser reads the top with nothing but the derived read key, and finds the access key inside. The reader pastes it once, on the first device; every other device gets it from the top.

• **The key pairs for this site.** At least a signing pair and an encryption pair, as [RFC 0001](../../../articles/rfc-0001-public-key-cryptography-for-sgit.md) separates them, and plausibly one per persona, so that what the CISO persona signs is not linkable to what the personal one signs. Each entry has a label, a purpose, a created date and a status. The public halves are published wherever the newsroom and the agent need them.

The key pairs are generated at random and stored. They are never derived from the passkey, and this is a decision, not an omission. A derived key pair cannot be rotated without changing the passkey, and you want several of them. More important, the passkey is a lock, not an identity: it opens the top and does nothing else. Everything that represents the person survives any change of lock, a new passkey, a second one, a hardware key, a recovery, a derivation bump. Rotate a lock and the identity is untouched; rotate an identity and the locks do not care. The trade-off against a non-extractable Web Crypto key is real and worth stating: a non-extractable key is stronger on one device, but it is one device, and an identity that has to be the same on the phone, the iPad and the iMac has to travel. An encrypted vault that only the passkey opens is the right vehicle for it. The private keys exist in browser memory only while the top is open.

Below the top, **the reading vault** holds one log per device, appended, never edited: pages read and how far, ratings, personas, the reading list, notes, receipts by payment reference. Every device computes the same state from all the logs, as described in [I miss it](../../../articles/i-miss-it.md).

### Several passkeys, several tops {#several}

A site can hold any number of passkeys for one person. Each passkey has its own PRF secret, so each computes its own top, and two passkeys are two independent trees. The facts that make this work, and the one that trips people up:

• **The store dedupes by user handle.** When a passkey is created, the site gives it a user id and a display name. iCloud Keychain and Google Password Manager treat a new passkey with the same user id for the same site as a replacement for the old one. So two passkeys that must coexist get two user ids and two names, "Dinis · admin" and "Dinis · reader". That is the whole trick.

• **The picker is the switch.** When the page asks for an assertion without naming a credential, the store shows its own sheet listing the passkeys it holds for this site, and the person picks one. That sheet is the interface for choosing which top to open; we do not build it. If the page remembers a credential id and a label in local storage, which are not secret, it can offer "Unlock admin" and ask for that passkey by id, with the sheet as the fallback.

• **Two stores in one browser.** In Chrome on a Mac the sheet offers both iCloud Keychain and Google Password Manager, plus a phone by QR and a hardware key, so one person can have a reader passkey in one store and an admin passkey in the other and switch between them on the same site in the same browser. Safari offers iCloud Keychain, hardware keys and a phone, not Google's store. Which of those paths returns PRF bytes in which browser is the thing the brief tests on a real machine rather than takes from a table.

The scenario this is for is separation of authority. An admin top holds what the desk needs: access keys, the write side of the newsroom's vaults, the publishing key pair. A reader top holds the reading vault, the notes vault and the persona key pairs. The admin passkey lives on a hardware key in a drawer, or in a different store from the reader one, so that the keys that can publish are not available every time the keys that can read are. The page shows which top is open, with a lock button that clears memory, and opens one top per tab by default.

**Moving keys between tops.** A top is a small file of entries, so a move is: unlock A, copy the entry into B, delete it from A. The catch is history. Vaults keep their versions, so an entry deleted from A is still in A's past for anyone who can open A. The rule: keys that move for security reasons get rotated, which for a vault key means `sgit rekey`, a new vault with a new id and the content re-pushed, and the references in every top updated; keys that move for tidiness do not; and a top being deleted takes its history with it.

**Retiring a top.** sgit can delete a vault from the server, `sgit vault delete-on-remote`, which needs the write key and a typed confirmation, and the vault's own files are gone. So the order is: move or rotate what the top held; delete the top's vault with its write key; delete the saved copy of its key from the password manager; then delete the passkey in the store's own settings, because a site cannot delete a passkey, only the person can. The coupling runs both ways and is worth noticing. Once the vault is deleted, the passkey still computes the same key, and the key opens nothing: a passkey whose vault is gone is inert. And once the passkey is deleted, the vault's ciphertext, if any survived, has no key. Deleting either side retires the pair. That is another reason to compute the top from the passkey rather than store its key: the lifecycle of the key is the lifecycle of the vault.

**Changing the derivation** is the same operation as adding a passkey: a new input gives a new top from the same passkey, the entries are copied across, the old top is retired. Nothing below the top moves.

For the newsroom, with the relying party ID `newsroom.sgit.ai`, as the lab runs it:

1. **The PRF input** is a fixed, public value: `SHA-256("newsroom.sgit.ai/door/v1")`. An input is not a secret; only the authenticator can turn it into the 32 bytes. 2. **The door seed** is `HKDF-SHA256(ikm = PRF bytes, salt = SHA-256("newsroom.sgit.ai"), info = "sgit/door/v1")`. 3. **The door's passphrase and vault id** are two more HKDF outputs from the seed. sgit accepts any printable ASCII passphrase up to 256 characters, so the passphrase is the hex of 32 bytes (`info = ".../passphrase"`), keeping all 256 bits. The vault id has to be lowercase letters and digits, 4 to 24 of them, so 8 characters are drawn from a third output (`info = ".../id"`) with rejection sampling, so that no character is favoured. The id is the door's address. 4. **The door vault key** is the sgit vault key made of those two, and from there, sgit's own derivation gives the read and write keys, exactly as the command line does: PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 at 600,000 iterations, once for the read key and once for the write key. That is the cost of this design. Door, master and reading vault need up to six derivations; measured in headless Chromium on a four-core machine, one takes about 105 ms and six run together about 640 ms, and a phone is several times slower, so a cold unlock can spend two to four seconds deriving keys before it fetches anything. The page derives each vault's keys once per session, runs them in a worker, and derives a write key only when there is something to write. 5. **The recovery door** is the same, with the recovery code in place of the PRF bytes: 26 characters of base32, 128 bits, made by the page and shown once. It is long so that it needs no password stretching, as in the secrets.sgit.ai keyring design. 6. **Collisions** are not a practical worry with 36⁸ possible ids, but the page checks: a derived address that already holds something it cannot open is skipped, with a counter in the HKDF info.

The browser and the command line agree byte for byte: the lab's test vectors run the same derivation from a fixed, fake PRF output through the browser code and through sgit in Python, and compare every value when the page opens.

### What is in each vault {#layout}

• **A door:** one file. The master vault's key, encrypted under the door's read key, and a small record: the kind of door (a passkey, or the recovery code), the provider as the browser named it, the path (platform or cross-platform), the credential id, which is public, a device label the reader typed, and the date.

• **The master vault:** the keyring. The keys of the vaults below it, by site and purpose: the reading vault first, then the notes-to-the-agent vault, then whatever an agent creates for the reader. Read keys the reader has been given. The access key: a read-only clone needs no token, so after the unlock the browser finds the access key here, and the reader pastes it once, on the first device. The key pairs for this site: a signing pair and an encryption pair, as [RFC 0001](../../../articles/rfc-0001-public-key-cryptography-for-sgit.md) separates them, and plausibly one per persona, each with a label, a purpose, a date and a status. And the list of doors, each with its own vault key, so that from any open door the page can read, rewrite or delete every other door.

• **The reading vault:** one log per device, appended, never edited: pages read and how far, ratings, personas, the reading list, notes, receipts by payment reference. Every device computes the same state from all the logs, as described in [I miss it](../../../articles/i-miss-it.md).

The key pairs are generated at random and stored. They are never derived from the passkey, and after the test that is more obviously right than it was: a key pair derived from bytes that depend on the path would be a different identity on the iPad than on the Mac. The passkey is a lock, not an identity. It opens a door and does nothing else. Everything that represents the person survives any change of lock, a new passkey, a second path, a hardware key, a recovery, a provider's fix. The trade-off against a non-extractable Web Crypto key is real: a non-extractable key is stronger on one device, but it is one device, and an identity that has to be the same on the phone, the iPad and the iMac has to travel. The private keys exist in browser memory only while the master is open.

### A door per path {#path}

The unit of the design is the path. Whatever produced a distinct set of bytes gets a distinct door: a passkey through its provider on the device, the same passkey through a phone over the hybrid link, a hardware key, a second passkey for the same role, the recovery code. Every door points at the same master and says where it came from.

**Adding a door moves no key through a person.** The page is unlocked, so the master's key is in its memory. The reader asks for the PRF bytes again by the other path. The page derives the new door from those bytes, encrypts the master's key under the new door's read key, writes the door's one file with the access key, and adds the door to the master's list. The provider that answered sees a PRF request and returns bytes; it never sees the master's key, a vault key or a passphrase. Nothing is typed, nothing is pasted, nothing public carries a key. A Mac with Chrome is where both paths run in one session, as run 4 showed: the provider on the Mac answers locally, and "use a phone, tablet or security key" reaches the same passkey over the hybrid link. So the setup for the phone-by-QR path is two gestures on the Mac, in the first week: open the door you have, then add the QR path as a door. Afterwards the iPad, or any browser that reaches the phone by QR, derives that door and finds the master.

**Where no device has both paths, the recovery code is the way in.** A new tablet whose only route is the QR path, before that path has a door, derives an address and finds nothing. The page says "no door here for this path yet" and offers two ways in: add the door from a device that is already open, or type the recovery code. The code derives the recovery door, which holds the master's key; the page is now unlocked; the new path's door is written as above. The recovery code is the one secret a person ever types, and only on a device where no door opens.

**An unknown address is not an error.** A derived address with nothing at it means a path with no door yet. The page never treats it as a failure, because a provider's fix can move a path's bytes at any time: if Apple or Google changes one path so that its bytes match the other, the door for the path that moved stops opening and the door for the other path takes over, with no loss. If a change moves a path's bytes to something new, that path finds no door, says so, and the reader adds one. The design never has to guess which output was correct. It only has to keep every door replaceable.

**Providers without PRF hold the recovery code, and are not doors.** A provider that returns no PRF bytes, Chrome's own store today and any password manager whose passkeys do not support the extension, cannot be a door, because there are no bytes to derive one from. It can hold the recovery code as a secure note. That makes it a holder of a door's passphrase, which is a weaker thing: whoever can read the note can open the recovery door. It is a fair place for the code for a reader who already trusts that manager with their passwords, and the page describes it as what it is.

**A lost device.** From any open door, delete the lost device's door, its file on the server and its entry in the list. That stops that path from finding the master from the next unlock on. It does not undo a copy of the master's key the lost device may have had in memory; the full answer is to rotate the master's key and rewrite the doors that are kept, which is designed and not built.

### Several passkeys, several masters {#several}

Doors are paths to one master. A second passkey for a different role is a second master, with its own doors. The facts that make this work, and the one that trips people up:

• **The store dedupes by user handle.** When a passkey is created, the site gives it a user id and a display name. iCloud Keychain and Google Password Manager treat a new passkey with the same user id for the same site as a replacement for the old one. So two passkeys that must coexist get two user ids and two names, "Dinis · admin" and "Dinis · reader".

• **The picker is the switch.** When the page asks for an assertion without naming a credential, the store shows its own sheet listing the passkeys it holds for this site, and the person picks one. If the page remembers a credential id and a label in local storage, which are not secret, it can offer "Unlock admin" and ask for that passkey by id, with the sheet as the fallback.

• **Two stores in one browser.** In Chrome on a Mac the sheet offers both iCloud Keychain and Google Password Manager, plus a phone by QR and a hardware key, so one person can have a reader passkey in one store and an admin passkey in the other, on the same site in the same browser. Safari offers iCloud Keychain, hardware keys and a phone, not Google's store.

An admin master holds what the desk needs: access keys, the write side of the newsroom's vaults, the publishing key pair. A reader master holds the reading vault, the notes vault and the persona key pairs. The admin passkey lives on a hardware key in a drawer, or in a different store from the reader one, so that the keys that can publish are not available every time the keys that can read are. The page shows which master is open, with a lock button that clears memory.

**Moving keys between masters.** A master is a small file of entries, so a move is: unlock A, copy the entry into B, delete it from A. The catch is history. Vaults keep their versions, so an entry deleted from A is still in A's past for anyone who can open A. The rule: keys that move for security reasons get rotated, which for a vault key means `sgit rekey`, a new vault with a new id and the content re-pushed, and the references in every master updated; keys that move for tidiness do not.

**Retiring, and the one thing never to destroy.** sgit can delete a file from a vault, and it can destroy a vault, `sgit vault delete-on-remote`, with the write key and a typed confirmation. A destroyed vault id can never be used again. That is the right tool for a master or a reading vault being retired for good, because their ids are random. It is the wrong tool for a door, because a door's address is derived from the passkey and the path: destroy it and that passkey can never open a door by that path again. So a door is retired by deleting its one file, and the address is left free for the day a door is wanted there again. Retiring a master is: move or rotate what it held, delete its doors' files, destroy the master and the vaults below it that are not kept, delete the saved recovery code, then delete the passkey in the store's own settings, because a site cannot delete a passkey, only the person can.

[figure pk-flows.webp] The first run, a new device, and a second passkey, a move and a retirement. Every step runs in the browser, against the user's passkey store for the gesture, and the vault server for ciphertext.

**First run.** Create a passkey for the site with `prf` enabled, named for its role; if the authenticator cannot do PRF, the page says which kinds can and offers another. Touch it: the PRF bytes give the top. Paste the access key. Generate the reading vault's key and the key pairs. Create the top and the reading vault. Move the reading account from the browser's storage into the reading vault. Show the top vault key once, behind "I have saved it in my password manager".

**A new device.** Touch the passkey, synced to this device or used from a phone by QR. The PRF bytes give the same top, the top gives the reading vault. Reading needs no access key; the access key comes out of the top, so this device can write as well. Merge this browser's reading into its own log.

**A second passkey.** Create it with a different user handle and name, in another store or on a hardware key. It computes its own top. Copy into it the entries it should hold, and nothing else.

**Lost a passkey.** Paste the saved top vault key; the top opens; create a new passkey, which computes a new top; copy the entries across; retire the old top in the order above.

[figure pk-flows.webp] The first device, a new device on a path that has a door, adding a door while unlocked, a new device on a path with no door yet, and a lost device. Every step runs in the browser, against the passkey store for the gesture and the vault server for ciphertext.

Once these dots are connected, we have something we did not have before: an end-to-end path from a gesture to a vault, entirely in the browser, on commodity pieces.pieces, and now tested against a real vault server. And just about every site and project we build needs exactly that.

2 unchanged paragraphs

• **One top,master, many vaults.** The reading vault is the first. The same topmaster can hold the key to [secrets.sgit.ai](https://secrets.sgit.ai/)'s keyring, a RiskMandate customer's policies, the memory of an agent the user runs, or the notes a reader sends to the newsroom.

• **Sharing without shared secrets.** The key pairs in the topmaster are what [RFC 0001](../../../articles/rfc-0001-public-key-cryptography-for-sgit.md) needs: give someone a vault key by encrypting it to their public key, with no secret sent in a chat.

• **One account across sites.** Two ways, later. A key hub, such as secrets.sgit.ai, holds the topmaster and hands a site only the key to its own vault, after the user approves it in a pop-up, the way a wallet connects to a site. Or, across different domains, WebAuthn's Related Origin Requests let one passkey work on a list of related sites, in Chrome and Safari today.

• **For anyone else.** None of this is specific to us. Any static site, on any host, could use a passkey with PRF and a vault, and give its users the same thing. I would like it to become a small, open component, the way [SG Meter](../../../articles/pay-after-you-read.md) is for reading.reading, and the lab is the start of it.

The design builds on secrets.sgit.ai's published design ([how it works](https://secrets.sgit.ai/how-it-works/), [the keyring format](https://secrets.sgit.ai/keyring/), [passkeys, WebAuthn and PRF](https://secrets.sgit.ai/learn/passkeys/) and [keys](https://secrets.sgit.ai/learn/keys/)), and on how sgit generates and parses vault keys in the client (`generate_vault_key` and `parse_vault_key`), deletesdestroys a vault (`sgit vault delete-on-remote`) and rotates a key (`sgit rekey`), read from the sgit command line's source; the unlock cost was measured with WebCrypto PBKDF2 in headless Chromium on 11 October 2026. The mismatch across paths is reported for iCloud Keychain on Apple's developer forums: [Different PRF output when using platform or cross-platform authentication attachment](https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/764730), [Passkey PRF inconsistency between Apple devices](https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/774111) and [PRF extension not supported in Safari's cross-device WebAuthn flow](https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/774112). The research: Corbado, [Passkeys and WebAuthn PRF for end-to-end encryption (2026)](https://www.corbado.com/blog/passkeys-prf-webauthn) and [WebAuthn L3 support in credential managers](https://www.corbado.com/blog/webauthn-l3-credential-manager-support); Yubico, [Developer's guide to PRF](https://developers.yubico.com/WebAuthn/Concepts/PRF_Extension/Developers_Guide_to_PRF.html); Mozilla, [support for the WebAuthn PRF extension](https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1863819); Chromium, [intent to ship the PRF extension](https://groups.google.com/a/chromium.org/g/blink-dev/c/iTNOgLwD2bI); web.dev, [passkey reuse across sites with Related Origin Requests](https://web.dev/articles/webauthn-related-origin-requests).
